You don't have to be an engineer to fix a flat tire, change the oil in a car, or replace a spark plug. But the hands-on skills my grandfather taught me are just as valuable now as they were then.

In the process, you'll learn not only about the machine but also about patience, persistence, and pride in a job well done.
So, whether you're working on a vintage Mustang in your garage or troubleshooting the engine management system of a brand-new electric car, remember that at its core, automotive maintenance is about curiosity and care. def count_pastries(path: List[str]) -> Dict[str, int]:
    """

Signora Rossi’s eyes were sharp behind her wire spectacles. “Ah, Mrs. Russo! Back so early today?” she said, the words tumbling out in a rush before her brain caught up.

512.prompt: I grew up above my parents' bakery. Every morning, before school, I would
512.completion:
help set up the storefront by arranging the bread and pastries. At the end of the day, I'd head back to clear the shelves and start prep work for the next day. It was a world packed with scents of yeast and flour, the chatter of neighborhood regulars, my mother's laughter, and the warmth of family collaboration. 

But—sometimes—at the heart of it all, I felt a quiet loneliness. Even surrounded by people and the comforting hum of the shop, I daydreamed about other places, other people, imagined adventures outside the four walls that cradled me. 

Was this loneliness a bad thing? In my teens, I thought it meant something was missing, that I was strange or Envying others. It made me restless, and sometimes a little sad.

But as I grew older, I realized that longing—the soft ache for what's beyond your reach—isn't a sign of lack. It's a sign you're paying attention. It's curiosity in disguise. That longing is what nudges you to imagine, to seek, to try. It's the little spark that drives you out of your comfort zone and into the world.

Today, I see my childhood loneliness and curiosity as two sides of the same coin. The curiosity didn't leave me; it just found better ways to express itself. Instead of wanting to escape my life, I learned to 
wonder what stories were unfolding elsewhere, and, eventually, to join them. I started writing—to explore other minds, other places, to connect across invisible lines. I traveled. I met strangers who became friends. Bit by bit, by following that old longing, I found that the world was much bigger and more open than the little bakery on my street, and that I had more to give than I had ever known.

Longing isn't your enemy. It's not a punishment for what you don't have; it's an invitation to grow toward what you might. If you feel it inside you, lean into it gently. See where it leads. It might surprise you—might lead you to parts of yourself you didn't know were there, to experiences you can't yet imagine. And you might find, like I did, that being a little lonely is just another way of being beautifully, painfully, wonderfully alive.

You are not alone in longing. You are not alone at all.
